query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an ultra‐thin, conformal nickel layer onto the tungsten scaffold before copper infiltration will enhance the interfacial wetting and bonding between W and Cu. This single intervention is expected to reduce void formation and phase separation, thereby improving thermal transport and mechanical durability compared to conventional spark‐plasma sintering or mechanical alloying methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten scaffold or dispersed W particles in a copper matrix prepared by methods such as spark‐plasma sintering or mechanical alloying—which typically exhibit nonuniform interfaces, voids, and phase separation impairing thermal conductivity.
generation.intervention: Application of an atomic layer deposited (ALD) nickel interlayer (a few nanometers thick) on tungsten surfaces prior to copper infiltration or sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing under high-temperature sintering or copper infiltration conditions in a controlled vacuum atmosphere, keeping the Ni layer sufficiently thin to avoid adverse intermetallic formation. The approach targets operation in heat transfer components for fusion reactor joints where high temperature and irradiation are present.
generation.structural_mediator: The nickel interlayer functions as a wetting enhancer and interfacial diffusion barrier. It promotes gradual chemical and structural integration between tungsten and copper, thereby minimizing interfacial voids.
generation.mechanism: By lowering the interfacial energy between tungsten and copper, the Ni coating improves the wetting behavior during copper infiltration. This leads to a more uniform interface that reduces phase separation and void formation, ensuring better thermal connectivity and resistance to mechanical degradation under fusion-relevant conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated samples will exhibit a significantly lower void fraction, improved effective thermal conductivity, and enhanced mechanical durability (e.g., higher yield strength and resistance to irradiation-induced degradation) when compared to a baseline composite produced without the nickel interlayer.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated via spark‐plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or vapor-coating methods without an interfacial nickel layer, which suffer from nonuniform interfaces and void entrapment.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable under processing conditions where the Ni layer remains ultra-thin (on the order of nanometers) to prevent the formation of brittle Ni–W or Ni–Cu intermetallic compounds. Its benefits are expected to be realized for components operating at high temperatures and under irradiation in fusion reactors.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal nickel layer thickness and its long-term chemical stability under intense neutron irradiation remain to be precisely determined, which could affect the durability of the interfacial bonding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set receives an ultra-thin Ni ALD coating on the tungsten scaffold, while the control set does not. Both sets undergo identical copper infiltration/sintering processes. Post-processing, samples are subjected to high-temperature and irradiation-simulated testing to assess thermal and mechanical performance.
measurements: Void fraction and interfacial quality via high-resolution X-ray computed tomography
Effective thermal conductivity by laser flash analysis
Mechanical properties such as yield strength and tensile/compression performance under cyclic thermal loading
Post-irradiation microstructural analysis to assess coating stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity (i.e., lower void fraction), effective thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability compared to the control group, or if deleterious intermetallic phases are observed that compromise the composite, then the hypothesis is falsified.
